today.name: Google EmbeddingGemma 2
today.tagline: An open, lightweight multimodal embedding model
today.description: EmbeddingGemma 2 is Google DeepMind's open embedding model that maps text, code, images, video and audio into one shared space, so you can search across them from a single query. At 740M parameters it runs on-device, needing about 567MB of RAM on a Pixel 11 Pro for the full multimodal model (191MB for text only). Apache 2.0 licensed, with weights on Hugging Face and Kaggle. MTEB Code score rises from 68.76 to 78.68.

comments.text: EmbeddingGemma 2 is Google DeepMind's open, lightweight multimodal embedding model. It maps text, code, images, video and audio into one shared space and is small enough to run on a phone.Problem: Searching by meaning usually needs a pipeline of separate models: a captioning model for images, speech-to-text for audio, a text embedder on top. That's slow, memory-hungry, and often sends your data to the cloud. For private, on-device apps, that's a hard trade-off.Solution: One 740M-parameter model, built on the Gemma 4 architecture, that embeds all five types of content in the same space. A text query can find a photo, and a voice memo can find a video clip. Everything runs locally, so your data never has to leave the device.What makes it different: It's modular. You can load only the encoders you need, as little as 270M parameters for text and code, plus optional vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders. With quantization on a Pixel 11 Pro, it needs about 191MB of RAM for text only and about 567MB for the full multimodal model. It shares its tokenizer and audio encoder with Gemma 4, so running both together uses less memory than running them separately.Key features:Text, code, images, video and audio in a single embedding space8K token context (4x EmbeddingGemma 1), enough for about 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images or 58 video framesVectors can be shrunk from 768 to 512, 256 or 128 dimensions for up to 6x less storageCode retrieval improves from 68.76 to 78.68 on MTEB Code (+9.92 points)Google says it leads sub-1B multimodal embedding models on benchmarks like MTEB Code and MAEB (audio)Can also act as a zero-shot, on-device decision engine: Google's MediaPipe demo scores 500 options per turn in a chess game in under 100 msWorks with transformers, sentence-transformers, MLX, vLLM, llama.cpp, SGLang, Ollama, LMStudio, Qdrant and UnslothWho it's for: Developers building private, offline-capable search, RAG, media retrieval or local codebase search, and anyone who wants cross-modal search without a cloud dependency. comments.text: Hi Product Hunt. Yuriy here, co-founder and CEO of AiSDR, 2x YC alumni. I once paid an outbound agency $30,000 and got zero meetings in 6 months. Then I built an AI SDR, sold it to 1,153 companies, and watched 80% of them get the same result, but faster and cheaper. The emails were fine. Nobody, including our software, solved the core problems - who should get them and why should they care to respond. AI SDR industry overpromised and underdelivered and people hated it. Ami is the thing I wish I could hand to every customer who trusted us in 2023 and got a fast way to fail. Here's what it looks like. You give it your website. It comes back with three campaign ideas, each with a signal behind it and a reason it thinks this one is likely to deliver results. That answer is not yet another AI slop. It's rooted in 17,707 campaigns we've run across 27 industries that booked 19,854 qualified meetings. You say "actually, I want every salesperson in Europe." It tells you that the audience has booked zero meetings across all campaigns we've run, and hands you the version that will. You say "I need 100 demos by October." It gives you the leads, the infrastructure, and the week the plan breaks if one of them slips. You approve. It builds campaigns and runs them across email and LinkedIn. When a campaign starts dying it tells you which of three things broke (audience, message, or timing), proposes a fix, fixes it for you and remembers what you chose. It also suggests new ideas as it learns more about you and your business. Full disclosure — I'm a big fan of Anthropic and actually built an app that works exclusively with Claude Desktop for secure local file search. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
